Why I built it: I wanted a simple, AI-platform-independent way to share and manage AI skills across teams, with features like editing permissions and version history.

mdkit is in beta and free to try on Windows and Mac.

story_text.value:
I made a daily game where you try to identify five Wikipedia articles by looking at their infoboxes with the name and picture hidden. You get one guess per article, and afterwards you get a summary and a link to Wikipedia so at least you might learn something even if you get it wrong!

Infoboxing was inspired by the Wikipedia guessing game Catfishing, which my friends and I love. We play as a group, which is probably cheating, but still sometimes only get like 3/10 correct. Part of the fun is discovering each person's niche and comparing our answers to the rest of the Catfishing audience on the stats page.

I've always wanted to make a daily game and I felt there was still room to explore in the Wikipedia guessing space. In my first prototype I picked out four or five rows from each infobox and revealed them one at a time, but making someone guess repeatedly at something they may never have heard of felt slow, especially across five articles. I ended up following Catfishing's approach: show all the clues with one guess or a skip.

My fiancée and I choose the articles. We started out listing everything we could think of, then explored Wikipedia lists like the "Unusual articles" page and also used AI to suggest candidates in areas we'd missed. In my opinion the best articles have an "a-ha!" moment where it suddenly clicks.

The hardest parts to get right are article curation, balancing the difficulty and deciding what counts as a correct answer. Should "Big Jesus" be an accepted answer for Christ the Redeemer? My fiancée thinks so! I've also put in some rules to try and keep a given day from being too difficult but ultimately it's based on vibes because my idea of what "everyone knows" is biased by my age, gender, region, etc.

The infoboxes are captured ahead of time so I set up a daily check to warn me if an article changes, mainly to catch things like ages changing or people dying. My favourite facepalm moment was when it warned me that Spock had died. His date of death on Wikidata? 2263.

Anyway, give it a go and see what you think. If you have an answer you think should count, tell me through the contact page so that we can keep spoilers out of the comments.

story_text.value:
Here's why I started building Sikemux:

At first I was using Cursor. The problem with it was, I had to open a new window for each project. That's when Zed came along. It was good and fast. But I didn't like its project switching much, it took me like 2 clicks instead of 1.

I had tried Cursor's agent-first feature as well, but didn't like it much, as I had to see files as well and do git ops with a good layout.

I had even tried tmux + sesh setups then.

That's when I started building Sikemux in Tauri. And project multiplexing got fast and solved, and I was able to see files and do git ops with a good layout of all.

Then came along the Codex App, its browser use and computer use was just tooo damn good, it got hard to go out of that app and try something else. And believe me when I say, I have tried all the ADEs out there. I had then forgot about Sikemux. But after using it for a while, I felt Codex App to be slow at times. It just screamed Electron to me, don't know though whether it's in Tauri or Electron.

I had to revive Sikemux. I then built all of it, great browser use! Fast project multiplexing, seeing files, doing git ops, connectors, agent orchestrator(chief), GUI, GPUI migration, macOS notch, remote hosts, working mobile app with iroh relay to stream everywhere, all in one beautiful window.

title.value: Show HN: Sikemux – a whole team of AI coders in one window (Rust, MIT)

story_text.value:
This is a web app that I built to introduce chess to my children, along with scratching a personal game analysis itch. I link to the games (free, ad free, tracker free, affiliate free, etc), though there is a full learning section as well that was my primary focus. I imagine many here already know the basics of chess.

Of course I leveraged AI in all parts of this project -- and indeed the analysis section uses three separate neural networks to analyze play -- but never without full engagement and co-working between myself and the machine (I've been doing web apps for 30+ years), and all designs are my own. I contrived several of the games wholesale, though others are well trodden in the chess world.

I use chess as a meditative beat from other engagements in my day to day, and have made it a personal mission to break out of the mediocre mid-tier play I've been stuck at for a few years. This has legitimately helped.

I hope this provides some enrichment for others.

story_text.value:
Rally is a multi-player platform to build reactive micro-applications together that connects event streams to agents that then update the artifact. We've had pilots build a PR dashboard that sorts by risk assessment (an agent actually reads the code) per PR, a micro-CRM that pulls in live deals from multiple Gmail inboxes, and a shared grocery list that groups items by store aisle.

We're similar to Muse's Spaces, Google's TableTop, and the standard artifacts most harnesses now support. Our differentiator is being multi-player so groups can iterate together, artifacts calling agents on incoming events so updates can be more sophisticated than an API call, and giving artifacts a full application stack.

Under the hood, each artifact is a Cloudflare Durable Object with its own SQLite database, compute, and storage.

As an example this is our podcast artifact that helps us keep up-to-date on what happened on the repo each day https://connected-tidy-crystalline-haldane-g.rallyuserconten...

GitHub: https://github.com/juno-ai-labs/avalon

title.value: Show HN: Open-source multi-player artifacts that update themselves

story_text.value:
We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

https://starsling.dev

story_text.value:
Jack lost his job as a software engineer to AI. To provide for his young family he takes a job as a lumberjack in Finland. The pay is good, the work engaging. It's good to be out in nature and work with his hands. He didn't ask what the land is for. With two kids, you don't ask.

A fun automation game in plain JavaScript, inspired by my memories of Warcraft (1994), Stardew Valley, the wonderful book Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow by Gabrielle Zevin and a little bit of Monty Python.

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I’m Sachin, and I’ve spent the last couple of months working on Faros Desktop, a Mac app that visualizes how you use your local AI coding tools into one place and then makes recommendations to make your subscription spend go further.

As agents have replaced hands-on-keyboard work, the team and I wanted to better understand what’s in our session traces. Faros Desktop hydrates with on-device session history in Codex, Claude Code, Github Copilot, and Cursor to let users deep dive into a beautiful visualization of AI session traces. Then based on consolidating that information, the app shows patterns in usage as well as recommendations for ways to save spend through simple changes that we call Power Ups.

Faros Desktop is totally free, with no login required and no API keys needed. The app also only uses on-device models to summarize local sessions in chunks, then organizes them by project and task. You can jump around a session timeline and see exactly the messages and tool calls in the trace.

The business model here for Faros Desktop is to drive thought leadership and create leads for our sales team to sell the company’s multi-player Token Engineering Platform for large engineering organizations. Faros has been serving large engineering organizations for the past seven years, so it was cool to be able to build a product for all Builders, not just enterprise engineering orgs.

One big direction we’re exploring: using previous sessions to make the next one better. We’re looking at local memory portability across harnesses as well as multi-player modes to share memory within your direct team. I’d love to hear thoughts on that.

Docs and product walkthrough: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/ Setup: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/getting-started/install-and-se... Data handling: https://docs.desktop.faros.ai/settings-and-privacy/understan... Faros website: https://www.faros.ai/

story_text.value:
I used Homepage for a while and it worked well enough for me but my wife kept saying it didn't work well on mobile or that she wanted to see our security cameras (Frigate), email, or media. I always joke that my wife is my most difficult end user to please, so her actually using it is already a win in my book.

I started thinking about how I could just combine the Home Assistant setup we've had for a few years with some practical home server pieces. Then just started thinking it'd be nice to create a place where I could have actionable server items (update containers, read RSS feeds, view cameras, see Dozzle's logs, etc.) all in one place with minimal configuration, so that I could check if backups completed successfully, see problems before they fail silently, and just learn some more.

I'm not a "traditional" software engineer, or would even consider myself one at all I suppose. In my current role I've been kind of expected to transition from data analytics/engineering and managing ETL pipelines into more full-stack development work, so I've done a lot of research about agentic coding and guardrails. I spend a while drawing out models, permissions, maps and flows on a whiteboard before ever prompting anything.

It's been fun and exciting but even I feel, as a non-developer, that there has to be a lot of work to frame everything correctly to get a tool that's useful, and I'd struggle to ever think anything I whip up should be sold to anyone.

Self-hosting and home automations have always been a hobby but AI has helped me create some internal tools at work or home that take existing services or platforms and consolidate them into one view, and that's the framework I applied to this.

Demo with fake data:

docker run --rm -p 3200:3200 -e DEMO=1 ghcr.io/sourpatchdad/patchboard:latest

title.value: Show HN: A dashboard my wife is finally interested in
